newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Lufthansa hopeful of higher 97 profit.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Lufthansa hopeful of higher 97 profit.

text.p: German airline Deutsche Lufthansa AG, seeking to recover from a 1996 slump, said on Wednesday it was hopeful it would report markedly higher 1997 profits after a first-quarter profit for the first time ever.

"Based on the performance in the first quarter, I hope we will achieve a pre-tax profit of more than 800 million marks ($464 million)," Weber said after a news conference in the Frankfurt airport terminal building.
Lufthansa said pre-tax earnings for the first quarter were 20 million marks -- almost 70 million marks better than first quarter 1996 when the group made a loss of 49 million marks.
Weber also said he was even more optimistic than he had been previously that the group would see a six-percent increase in sales.

Shares in Lufthansa rose in bourse trading to end up 85 pfennigs, around 3.26 percent, at 26.85 marks, just off a year high of 27.05 marks and outpacing losses in the blue-chip DAX index which ended down 16.30 points at 3,551.98 points.
The share ended afternoon electronic trade on the IBIS DAX index up 49 pfennigs, or 1.81 percent, at 26.98 marks.

"The first quarter has ended in profit for the first time in the airline's history. In our part of the world, it is normally a loss-maker," said Lufthansa chief executive Juergen Weber at the news conference.

But the entire pre-tax profit came from financial operations, which includes income from subsidiaries and associated companies. It had an operating loss of one million marks compared with a 49 million mark loss last year.
Group turnover in the first three months climbed 8.5 percent to almost five billion marks, with 90 percent of the sales coming from passengers and freight.
The balance of the group's revenues came from Lufthansa's aero-engineering services and its LSG catering business, raising the group's total sales to 5.28 billion marks.

The airline in 1996 reported a profit from ordinary activities of 686 million marks, down nine percent from 756 million marks in 1995 despite a nearly five percent rise in group turnover to 22.9 billion marks.
Lufthansa said its 1996 results were burdened by nearly 680 billion marks attributed to surging fuel costs, a sharp rise in airport fees and a one-off charge for pension provisions.
But Lufthansa said it has already made good the downturn in earnings in 1996 in the first three months of the year.
Lufthansa also said it had realised 200 million marks in savings in 1996 from its alliances with other airlines and would make further savings this year.

"We expect clearly higher savings in 1997 from alliances," the airline said in a statement, noting its alliance with Scandinavian Airlines System SAS alone had led to savings of hundreds of millions of marks.
Lufthansa has built the code-share alliance with major partners United Airlines of the U.S., Thai International Airways, SAS and South African Airways.
Weber also said on Wednesday the airline was interested in building a similar alliance for its cargo operations.

The higher first-quarter profit figure came as traffic revenue incrased about nine percent to 4.4 billion marks despite only a 1.3 percent rise in the number of passengers and only a 1.7 percent increase in freight business volumes.
"The increase in turnover was due mainly to improved yields on both passenger and cargo operations," the airline said.

Lufthansa also said its fuel costs were also sharply higher, rising 37 percent to 524 million marks but noted a markedly smaller increase in total operating expenditure, which rose seven percent to 5.28 billion marks.
--Frankfurt Newsroom, +49 69 756525 ($ = 1.723 German Marks)
